title: Tarn Taran, 1921
hook: reformers were attacked seeking to take over the gurdwara

segments.voice: Yesterday, the SGPC, and your line was volunteers stepped up. Did you do the task nobody asked for? Today, the volunteers arrive at a gurdwara, and it goes badly. Day nine hundred eighty-four.

Early in 1921, a band of reformers walks into a town south of Amritsar, where a gurdwara stands beside a wide sacred pool. Tradition says Guru Arjan founded the town. They have come, singing, to ask the priests who hold the shrine to hand it over to the Panth. They talk, and they wait to be heard. Night falls. They're still there, waiting, when the priests' men come at them with weapons. Today: Tarn Taran.
screen: `A SACRED POOL SOUTH OF AMRITSAR.` → `REFORMERS COME TO TALK.` → `AT NIGHT, AN ATTACK.`

segments.voice: First, why they came. The custodians at Tarn Taran were accused by the reformers of allowing practices in the shrine that went against the Gurus' teaching, and of treating its offerings as their own. The reformers came to take over its management for the newly formed committee. Second, the attack. Accounts say that while they waited, the priests and the men with them attacked the reformers, who were struck with sticks and blades. Several were badly wounded, and some died of their wounds. Third, the response. The reformers did not answer the attack with an attack. They held their ground, cared for the wounded, and the shrine in the end passed to the Panth's management. Calm, here, did not mean quiet. It meant not letting someone else's violence choose your next move. Fourth, the Guru's line. Guru Tegh Bahadur, in a salok at Ang 1427 of the Guru Granth Sahib, praises the one who frightens no one and fears no one. Both halves matter. The reformers came without frightening anyone, and they didn't run when they were frightened. Tradition explains the name Tarn Taran as a boat that carries people across. That night, the people who came to the pool needed something to carry them through. They found it in staying still. That's today's line.
screen: `THEY CAME TO TAKE OVER THE SHRINE.` · `AT NIGHT, STICKS AND BLADES.` · `THEY HELD THEIR GROUND.` · `FRIGHTEN NO ONE, FEAR NO ONE.` · then, large: `CALM UNDER ATTACK.`

segments.voice: Two minutes to practice calm in conflict. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind a recent argument, or a moment when someone came at you with sharp words. Notice whether your body reacts even now: the jaw, the shoulders, the chest. Breathe in slowly. On the breath out, let the jaw go. Again, and let the shoulders drop. This isn't giving in. It's refusing to let the other person's anger set your pace. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Tarn Taran. A gurdwara town south of Amritsar, where reformers who came to talk were attacked at night and held their ground. Today's word.
Your line: calm under attack. Today, the next time someone comes at you sharply, take one full breath before you answer. Day nine hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Sikhs visit the gurdwara at Tarn Taran, with its large sarovar, as a historic shrine; the reformers who died there are remembered among the martyrs of the gurdwara reform movement.
